Section 1  
The Twitterverse erupted when Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt found himself locked in an unexpected feud with comedian Ralf Little over the state of NHS mental healthcare. The clash began after Hunt appeared on *The Andrew Marr Show*, boldly declaring that the NHS had achieved “the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe.” Little, famed for his role in *The Royle Family*, swiftly called out the claim in a fiery tweet, accusing Hunt of “knowingly lying” to the public. Challenging Hunt’s credibility, Little dared the minister to sue him if the statistics he cited were accurate—a provocation that set the stage for a highly publicized war of words.  

Section 2  
Hunt’s assertion had already drawn scrutiny. Just weeks earlier, he had admitted to misstating the number of new mental health workers, initially claiming a rise of 30,000—a figure later revealed to be 43 times the actual count. Now, under renewed pressure, Hunt fired back at Little with a barrage of statistics, “double daring” the actor to disprove him. “You’re a comedian, but this isn’t a joke,” Hunt tweeted, linking to datasets he argued supported his position. The exchange quickly escalated, with Hunt framing it as a battle over truth in public discourse, while critics noted his history of inflated claims.  

Section 3  
Undeterred, Little launched a meticulous rebuttal, publishing a 40-tweet thread dissecting Hunt’s assertions. He cited analyses from Full Fact, an independent UK fact-checking organization, to highlight discrepancies in the health secretary’s data. One key point: Hunt’s cited “expansion” relied on reclassifying existing staff roles rather than new hires. Little’s thread, peppered with sarcastic asides and hard-hitting evidence, went viral, amassing over 15,000 shares. Supporters praised his tenacity, with many calling it a masterclass in holding power to account.  

Section 4  
Hunt retaliated with a 26-tweet marathon of his own, though critics noted his thread devolved into confusion when he lost chronological order mid-rant. He doubled down on his stance, insisting mental health reforms were “on track” and highlighting 8,000 mental health nurses in training. Crucially, he cited a *New York Times* article to bolster his case—only for opponents to remind him the piece had been corrected three times after Luciana Berger, former shadow minister for mental health, flagged inaccuracies. Hunt’s attempt to weaponize the article backfired, raising fresh doubts about his grasp of the facts.  

Section 5  
As the feud dominated headlines, public opinion split. Some lauded Little for exposing political spin, while others dismissed the spat as trivializing serious healthcare issues. Behind the memes and retweets, the clash underscored deeper tensions: crumbling NHS mental health services, staffing shortages, and a public weary of statistical sleight-of-hand. With Hunt refusing to concede ground and Little vowing to keep fighting, the row became a cautionary tale about the perils of politics meeting social media—where facts, once tangled, are harder to untangle than a Twitter thread.
